description_full: ArcelorMittal S.A., together with its subsidiaries, operates as integrated steel and mining companies in the Americas, Europe, Asia, and Africa. It offers semi-finished flat products, including slabs; finished flat products comprising plates, hot- and cold-rolled coils and sheets, hot-dipped and electro-galvanized coils and sheets, tinplate, and color coated coils and sheets; semi-finished long products, such as blooms and billets; finished long products consisting of bars, wire-rods, structural sections, rails, sheet piles, and wire-products; and seamless and welded pipes and tubes. The company also provides mining products, such as iron ore lumps, fines, concentrate, pellets, and sinter feeds; and coking coal. It sells its products to various customers in the automotive, appliance, engineering, construction, energy, and machinery industries through a centralized marketing organization, and distributors. The company operates iron ore mining activities in Brazil, Bosnia, Liberia, Mexico, South Africa, and Ukraine, as well as in India and in Canada. ArcelorMittal S.A. was founded in 1976 and is headquartered in Luxembourg, Luxembourg.

financial_summary: Arcelor Mittal NY Registry Shar is a large-cap basic materials business with a $45.9B market cap on $61.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -8% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 6% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 9% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $471M in free cash flow — roughly 1 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.48× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.0× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.3×.

Shareholder yield is only 1.2%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Basic Materials median (10%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.45x its revenue share).
It accounts for 3.7% of sector revenue and 1.7% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+1.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 75% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 17% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 23% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 44% and a beta of 1.15, it moves roughly with the market.
About $87.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 61% in the 2020 crash, 46% in the 2022 bear market and 85% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $39.09 (margin of safety -56%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 46%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $26.46 to $57.29 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/E 44.5 vs 16.5, EV/EBITDA 20.7 vs 8.5 and P/FCF 97.4 vs 22.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 166% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $77.80 on average, 28% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.04).
It runs a 9% gross margin and converts 1% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.48x.
ROE of 6% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.0x net debt to EBITDA ($5.4B of cash against $11.8B of debt), with interest covered 6.3x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -8.4% over 3 years and 2.9% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 19%).
At current returns, reinvesting 59% of profits supports about 3.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -22.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 16.9% on average.
Analysts expect 81.7% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 5%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.2% (1.0% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 7.1% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 125,554 employees, each generates about $489K of revenue, 0.8x the Basic Materials median.
That works out to $4K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
Compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
